**General Practices:**

1. Graded Practice – Identifying and Eliminating fluff from questions.  
2. Leading with limited information.   
3. Using State Lab Investigations as sample data for clusters.  
4. Old Regents Questions for check-ins, use clusters and those in tandem

Short answer: **no, quarks and the internal composition of the proton are not required by the NYS Physics curriculum.** Let me give you the longer answer because the boundary is worth understanding clearly.

**What the NYSSLS Physical Science standards actually require regarding subatomic structure:**

The standards — HS-PS2 (Forces & Motion), HS-PS3 (Energy), HS-PS4 (Waves & EM), plus HS-PS1-8 and HS-ESS1-2 — do not mention quarks, the Standard Model, or the internal structure of nucleons anywhere. The closest the standards come to subatomic structure is **HS-PS1-8**, which asks students to "develop models to illustrate the changes in the composition of the nucleus and the energy released during the processes of fission, fusion, and radioactive decay." The clarification statement and assessment boundary for HS-PS1-8 explicitly limit this to **basic fission, fusion, and radioactive decay processes** — the model is the proton/neutron/nucleus level, not the quark level.

The NGSS framework that NYSSLS is built on does mention quarks in the underlying *Framework for K-12 Science Education* (the Disciplinary Core Idea PS1.A includes brief language about how protons and neutrons are themselves made of smaller particles called quarks), but this language was deliberately **not pulled into the performance expectations**. The framework treats quarks as background context for the writers, not as content students are accountable for.

Even when not strictly required, a brief introduction to quarks (one class period, maybe two) is worth including because it (a) appears on every Regents Physics reference table students may encounter, (b) connects beautifully to HS-PS1-8 nuclear processes when you discuss what holds protons together (the strong force, mediated by gluons binding quarks), and (c) is genuinely interesting to students in a way that motivates the broader modern physics unit. Treat it as a 30-minute conceptual introduction rather than a topic students need to master computationally.
